blocks.text: Pediatric limits depend on the assay and the population behind them. Use your laboratory's age- and sex-specific range. This card lists only limits or thresholds a guideline or population study publishes, and says which is which; where none exists, it says so.

Direct bilirubin > 1.0 mg/dL (17 µmol/L) is abnormal at any total: start the cholestasis workup and refer to pediatric hepatology (NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN 2017). This is a disease threshold, not a normal range. It applies to direct bilirubin; conjugated assays read lower — use your laboratory's conjugated cut-off.

sub: Highest in newborns; falls over the first year to low childhood values.
In a cholestatic infant, a GGT normal for age is the finding: think PFIC 1 and 2 (and other low-GGT forms) and bile acid synthesis defects.
Follows bone growth: high through childhood, peaks in puberty (girls earlier than boys).
An adult upper limit makes every growing child look cholestatic.
Isolated high ALP: check GGT first, then vitamin D.
Very high ALP in a well toddler with normal GGT: think transient hyperphosphatasemia (benign).
Also from muscle and red cells: check CK and hemolysis before blaming the liver.
Isolated high AST with normal CK and no hemolysis: think macro-AST.
Beyond the newborn period: no pediatric guideline limit. Use the laboratory range.

items: Crying, struggling and seizures raise it falsely.
Put the sample on ice and send it at once; analyze within 1 hour.

items.text: Direct is not conjugated: the 1.0 mg/dL cut-off is for direct bilirubin. Conjugated assays read lower — use your laboratory's conjugated cut-off.
Low ALP for age is abnormal too: think hypophosphatasia, zinc deficiency and, with jaundice and hemolysis, Wilson acute liver failure.
ALT 22/26 U/L is a health-based cut-off for teens, not the laboratory's reference interval.
AFP at birth runs in the tens of thousands and halves about every 5 days in the first month. Judge it against age, and follow the trend.
A normal ammonia virtually excludes a urea cycle disorder in a symptomatic newborn, but not in an older child.
